scope: Type-free threshold uniqueness from maxima and Gauduchon Stokes

edits.old: Multiplier-ideal data will also give a uniqueness criterion for equations. Under the smooth semipositive Gauduchon maximizer hypothesis of \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation}, threshold subsolutions are unique modulo constants within each multiplier-ideal class. The proof first shows that their difference has divisorial curvature supported on the analytic degeneracy set. Equality of generic Lelong numbers then removes every coefficient. This uses the special equation and dual hypothesis; equality of multiplier ideals alone does not control Monge--Amp\`ere mass.

At a positive threshold and in dimension at least two, \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} allows a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives the exact global equation and smoothness off $Z$. Differences of solutions are divisorial and satisfy a Bott--Chern relation. Consequently uniqueness holds within each multiplier-ideal class, or without prescribing a class when the divisor classes are independent, in particular if $Z$ has codimension at least two. This does not give global regularity or capacity convergence of the normalized exponential solutions.
edits.new: At a positive threshold and in dimension at least two, \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} allows a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives the exact global equation, smoothness off $Z$, and uniqueness of all threshold subsolutions modulo constants. The uniqueness proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to remove the resulting nonpositive divisorial difference. It requires no prescribed singularity type or independence of divisor classes. This does not give global regularity or capacity convergence of the normalized exponential solutions.

edits.old: Strict positivity of a smooth maximizing form can be weakened if its degeneracy is confined to a proper analytic subset. The proof is local away from that subset. The possible ambiguity of the potential is then divisorial.
edits.new: Strict positivity of a smooth maximizing form can be weakened if its degeneracy is confined to a proper analytic subset. The proof is local away from that subset. A maximum argument and a Gauduchon integral then give uniqueness without prescribing a singularity type.

If $u,v$ are threshold subsolutions and $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ are the prime divisorial components of $Z$, there are real numbers $c_j$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:semipositive-dual-divisorial-difference}
 \ddc(u-v)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j[Z_j],\qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^m c_j\{Z_j\}=0
       \quad\text{in }H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R).
\end{equation}
Consequently threshold solutions are unique modulo constants within each multiplier-ideal equivalence class, hence within each ordinary singularity type. They are unique modulo constants without a prescribed type if the classes $\{Z_j\}$ are linearly independent. In particular this holds when $Z$ has codimension at least two.
edits.new: All threshold subsolutions differ by constants.

edits.new:
For $q=u$ or $q=v$, the current $S=\ddc(w-q)$ is real, closed, of order zero and supported on $Z$. The classical support theorem, \cite[Chapter III, Corollaries 2.11 and 2.14]{DemCADG}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:semipositive-dual-divisorial-difference}
 S=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j[Z_j],\qquad
 c_j=\nu(w,Z_j)-\nu(q,Z_j)\leq0,
\end{equation}
where $Z_j$ are the prime divisorial components of $Z$. Indeed, near a generic smooth point of $Z_j$, the difference $w-q-c_j\log|z_1|^2$ is pluriharmonic, since $\ddc\log|z_1|^2=[Z_j]$ in our normalization. This identifies the coefficient; its sign follows from $w\geq q$. Higher-codimension components carry no closed order-zero $(1,1)$-current.

edits.old: The expression in parentheses is a smooth pluriharmonic function by distributional elliptic regularity. Taking generic Lelong numbers therefore gives $c_j=\nu_{Z_j}(u)-\nu_{Z_j}(v)$. If $u\sim_{\mathcal I}v$, these numbers agree by \cref{thm:local-i-inputs}, so all coefficients vanish. Ordinary equivalence implies multiplier-ideal equivalence. Alternatively, independence of the divisor classes forces them all to vanish directly from \eqref{eq:semipositive-dual-divisorial-difference}. In either case $\ddc(u-v)=0$ globally, and a real pluriharmonic distribution on connected compact $X$ is constant. When $Z$ has codimension at least two, the sum is empty.
edits.new: Each divisor integral is positive and each $c_j$ is nonpositive, so every coefficient vanishes. Therefore $w-q$ is a global pluriharmonic distribution and is constant on connected compact $X$. Applying this to both $q=u$ and $q=v$ shows that $u-v$ is constant.

edits.old: The theorem assumes a smooth form. It neither defines a wedge product with an arbitrary singular maximizing current nor proves that such a current has an analytic degeneracy set. The divisor relation is necessary for two threshold solutions to differ; it does not assert that every relation is realized. No bounded mass, positive lower mass, root-tail condition, or convergence of an exponential approximation is used.
